items.prompt: How does a placenta feed a developing mammal before it is born?

options.label: It links the mother's blood supply closely to the young's own
options.feedback: Nutrients and oxygen cross from her blood to the young's across a thin barrier, and waste crosses back the other way, without the two bloods ever mixing.

options.label: It stores food eaten during pregnancy for the young to draw on later
options.feedback: The connection works continuously, meal by meal, rather than banking a single store for the young to use whenever it wants.

options.label: It pumps digested food directly into the young's stomach
options.feedback: The young's own digestive system stays unused before birth. Nutrients arrive already broken down, through the blood, not through a stomach.

options.label: It filters the mother's blood into a separate reservoir the young drinks from
options.feedback: There is no reservoir. Exchange happens directly across the placenta's surface as blood from each side passes close together.

items.ok_line: A close link between two bloodstreams, never quite touching.
items.ko_line: Think about how directly and continuously the connection works, rather than picturing a store being built up.
items.exp_title: Two bloodstreams, kept apart but close
items.exp_text: The placenta grows against the wall of the mother's womb and brings her blood vessels into close contact with those of the developing young, close enough that oxygen and nutrients cross a thin barrier from her side to the young's, while carbon dioxide and waste cross back the other way. The two bloodstreams themselves never mix, which matters because the mother's blood and the young's can carry different antibodies and even different blood types. This exchange runs continuously for as long as the young is developing inside her.

items.prompt: Why is a newborn kangaroo blind, hairless and barely developed at birth?

options.label: It finishes most of its development later, nursing in the pouch
options.feedback: Born after only a very short time inside the mother, it crawls unaided into the pouch and locks onto a teat, completing its growth there instead.

options.label: Something went wrong during its mother's pregnancy
options.feedback: Every kangaroo is born this undeveloped. It is the normal pattern for the species, not a sign that anything failed.

options.label: It was born prematurely by accident
options.feedback: There is no accident here. A kangaroo pregnancy is simply built to end this early as a matter of course.

options.label: Its mother cannot produce enough milk before birth
options.feedback: Milk production only begins once the young starts nursing. Milk supply has nothing to do with how developed the young is at birth.

items.ok_line: Development finished outside the womb, in the shelter of a pouch instead.
items.ko_line: This is not a mistake or a mishap. It is simply how a kangaroo pregnancy is built to end.
items.exp_text: A kangaroo, like other marsupials, carries its young inside the womb for only a short time before giving birth to something closer to an early embryo than a finished newborn. That tiny, still-forming joey then crawls on its own through its mother's fur into the pouch, where it clamps onto a teat and stays attached for months, continuing to grow and develop there in a kind of second, external stage of pregnancy. Much later, it opens its eyes, grows fur and finally begins to leave the pouch on its own.

items.prompt: Why is a mother mammal's very first milk different from the milk she produces later?

options.label: It is packed with antibodies that protect the newborn from disease
options.feedback: This early milk, called colostrum, hands over ready-made defences the newborn's own immune system has not yet had time to build.

options.label: It contains no fat, to protect the newborn's digestion
options.feedback: Early milk actually tends to be rich rather than thin. What sets it apart is its load of protective compounds, not an absence of fat.

options.label: It is thinner and more watery, easier to swallow
options.feedback: This early milk is usually thicker than ordinary milk, not thinner, because of everything concentrated into it.

options.label: It is produced in much larger quantities than later milk
options.feedback: Quantity is not the distinguishing feature here. A newborn only needs small amounts at a time, and what matters is what that milk carries.

items.ok_line: A first dose of ready-made immunity, delivered before the newborn can build any of its own.
items.ko_line: Think about what the newborn is missing in its very first hours that this milk could supply directly.
items.exp_title: A first dose of borrowed immunity
items.exp_text: A newborn mammal's own immune system has had no chance yet to encounter anything and build up defences, leaving it vulnerable in its first days. To cover that gap, a mother's first milk, called colostrum, is loaded with antibodies drawn from her own immune system, which the newborn's gut can absorb intact in the earliest hours after birth. Within a day or two, that gut loses the ability to absorb antibodies whole, and the milk itself shifts toward its ordinary, longer-term composition.

items.prompt: Why can a newborn foal stand up and walk within an hour of being born?

options.label: It is born with limbs and a brain mature enough for immediate movement
options.feedback: Development that another animal would finish after birth has already happened inside the womb, so the foal arrives ready to bear its own weight straight away.

options.label: Its mother physically lifts it onto its feet
options.feedback: A mare does not lift her foal upright. The foal manages this entirely under its own strength, using legs already developed enough for the job.

options.label: Its bones are unusually light, making standing effortless
options.feedback: A foal's legs carry its full weight from the very start, which calls for sturdy bone and muscle, not unusually light ones.

options.label: It has extra joints that make balancing easier
options.feedback: A foal's legs have the same joints as any horse's. What lets it stand so soon is how developed those legs already are, not any extra joint.

items.ok_line: A body finished enough at birth to get straight to work.
items.ko_line: Think about how much development has already happened before birth, rather than about any single body part.
items.exp_text: A horse spends a long pregnancy in which the muscles, bones and nervous system needed for movement are already largely finished by the time of birth, unlike species that are born to complete much of that growth afterward. Standing and walking almost immediately matters for a grazing animal on open ground, where a foal unable to keep up with the herd would be an easy target. This pattern of arriving ready to move is common among plant-eating animals that live exposed rather than hidden away.

items.prompt: Why are newborn mice born blind, hairless and completely helpless?

options.label: Their mother invests less in development before birth and more after
options.feedback: A short pregnancy delivers the young early and unfinished, and the remaining growth happens afterward, fed and sheltered in the safety of a nest.

options.label: Something interrupted their development in the womb
options.feedback: This is the normal outcome for every mouse pregnancy, not an interruption or a problem.

options.label: Mice cannot produce milk rich enough to finish development in the womb
options.feedback: Milk is used after birth, not before. It has no bearing on how far development gets while the young are still inside the mother.

options.label: Mice are simply too small to grow further before birth
options.feedback: Body size on its own does not decide how developed a newborn is. Small mammals exist on both ends of this pattern, some helpless at birth and others fully mobile.

items.ok_line: Less finished before birth, and made up for afterward, safe inside a nest.
items.ko_line: Nothing has gone wrong here. This is simply where a mouse's pregnancy is built to stop, with the rest of development to follow.
items.exp_title: A short pregnancy, a long recovery
items.exp_text: A mouse pregnancy lasts only a few weeks, ending well before the muscles, fur and senses needed for independence have finished forming, and the newborn arrives blind, naked and unable to regulate its own body heat. What it lacks in prenatal development, it makes up afterward, hidden in a nest and fed on milk while its mother's own body is freed up sooner to breed again. This pattern trades a short, low-cost pregnancy for weeks of intensive care once the young are already born.

items.prompt: How does growing up in a herd of female relatives help an elephant calf?

options.label: Aunts and older sisters help watch, comfort and guide it, not only its mother
options.feedback: With several experienced adults sharing the work of caring for it, the calf gets more protection and guidance than one mother alone could provide.

options.label: Every female in the herd produces milk for it
options.feedback: Only the calf's own mother nurses it in the ordinary case. What the other females contribute is protection and guidance, not milk.

options.label: The herd's size alone keeps predators from noticing it
options.feedback: A large herd is not hidden by its size; it is defended by it. Older females actively drive predators off rather than simply going unnoticed.

options.label: Related females take turns carrying it while it is small
options.feedback: An elephant calf walks on its own from soon after birth. It is never carried by other members of the herd.

items.ok_line: More than one adult sharing the work of watching and guiding a single calf.
items.ko_line: Think about what the other females contribute that a single mother, working alone, could not supply as easily.
items.exp_text: An elephant calf grows up surrounded by its mother, aunts, older sisters and a grandmother figure, and these related females share the work of watching over it, stepping in to comfort it if it strays or shield it if a predator approaches. Older females that have raised calves before also pass on knowledge, such as where to find water in a drought, that the calf absorbs simply by staying close to the group as it grows. A calf raised this way has far more attentive adults around it than a mother managing entirely on her own could ever provide.

items.prompt: How does a mother mammal, such as a seal on a crowded beach, tell her own young apart from hundreds of others?

options.label: She recognises its individual scent
options.feedback: Each young mammal carries a distinct scent, and a mother learns it soon after birth, using it to pick her own out of a crowd by smell alone.

options.label: She recognises it by the sound of its cry alone
options.feedback: Calls can help draw a mother and young closer together, but confirming the match at close range still relies on something more certain: scent.

options.label: She marks her young with a scratch or bite at birth
options.feedback: No mammal makes a lasting mark this way. Recognition instead relies on a scent that is already unique to the young from birth.

options.label: She simply stays near the spot where she gave birth
options.feedback: A crowded beach shifts constantly as animals move around, so location alone could not reliably keep a mother paired with her own young.

items.ok_line: A scent unique to one animal, learned and never forgotten.
items.ko_line: Calls help two animals find each other from a distance, but think about what confirms the match once they are close.
items.exp_title: Recognition by scent, confirmed up close
items.exp_text: Many mammal mothers memorise the particular scent of their own young in the hours right after birth, an imprint that stays sharp for as long as the young needs her. Calls can help mother and young locate one another across a crowded space, but the final check, before a mother allows nursing, is almost always a close sniff to confirm the scent matches. A seal that approaches the wrong pup on a beach packed with hundreds of them will be driven off the moment that sniff fails to match.

items.prompt: Why does the platypus lay eggs, unlike almost every other mammal?

options.label: It belongs to an ancient branch of mammals that never evolved a placenta
options.feedback: Splitting off from other mammals very early on, its lineage kept the ancestral habit of laying eggs rather than developing the placenta most mammals rely on today.

options.label: It is not really a mammal
options.feedback: It nurses its young on milk, has fur and is warm-blooded, which makes it a mammal in every sense that matters, egg-laying included.

options.label: Its body is too small to carry developing young
options.feedback: Plenty of much smaller mammals carry young to birth without laying eggs. Body size is not what decides this.

options.label: It lives partly in water, where eggs survive better
options.feedback: Plenty of fully aquatic mammals, such as whales, give live birth without any trouble. A watery habitat does not require laying eggs.

items.ok_line: A line of mammals that branched off before the placenta was ever invented.
items.ko_line: This is a very old lineage, one that split away from other mammals a long time before most of today's mammal traits appeared.
items.exp_title: A branch that split off before the placenta
items.exp_text: The platypus belongs to a small group called monotremes, whose ancestors separated from the rest of the mammal family tree before the placenta, the organ that lets most mammal young develop fully inside the womb, had evolved. Lacking that structure, a monotreme still relies on an egg to nourish its young through the earliest stage of development, much as reptile ancestors once did. Once the egg hatches, though, the young feeds in an entirely mammalian way, on milk that oozes from patches of skin rather than through a proper teat.

items.prompt: Why do young mammals spend so much time in play, such as chasing, wrestling or stalking?

options.label: Play lets them practise adult skills safely, without real danger
options.feedback: A mock chase or a play fight rehearses the same movements a real hunt or escape will need, at a stage when getting it wrong costs nothing.

options.label: Young mammals have extra energy with nowhere else to go
options.feedback: Surplus energy might explain restlessness in general, but it does not account for why play so consistently mimics adult behaviours like chasing and pouncing.

options.label: Play helps them grow their fur in faster
options.feedback: Fur growth is controlled by hormones and development, entirely separate from anything an animal does through activity or play.

options.label: Adults teach play as a way to establish dominance early
options.feedback: Play between young animals is usually mutual and repeated by both sides, not a one-sided lesson in rank imposed by an adult.

items.ok_line: Rehearsal for adult life, run at a stage when mistakes carry no real cost.
items.ko_line: Notice how closely play mimics the exact movements of chasing, fighting or catching prey. That resemblance is the clue.
items.exp_text: A young mammal at play so often chases, pounces, wrestles or stalks because those are the very movements it will need as an adult, whether to catch food, escape a predator or compete with rivals. Practising them now, while the consequences of a clumsy attempt are harmless, lets the muscles, timing and coordination for these skills develop and sharpen well before they are needed for real. A kitten pouncing on a moving leaf is drilling the same motion an adult cat will later use on genuine prey.

items.prompt: Why does an orca calf stay close to its mother for years rather than becoming independent quickly?

options.label: It has a great deal of hunting knowledge to learn from her
options.feedback: Techniques for finding and catching particular prey are passed down by example over years, not absorbed in a single season.

options.label: Its body takes years just to grow large enough to swim
options.feedback: A calf can already swim competently within its first days of life. Growth rate is not what keeps it by its mother's side so long.

options.label: Orca mothers physically prevent their calves from leaving
options.feedback: A calf stays close by its own choice, following and learning, rather than being restrained or kept from swimming off.

options.label: It needs years to develop the ability to breathe air
options.feedback: Breathing air through the blowhole works from birth. It is not something that takes years of development to manage.

items.ok_line: Years spent learning techniques that took her own lifetime to build up.
items.ko_line: The calf can already swim and breathe from the start. Ask what it still cannot do without watching her closely.
items.exp_text: An orca hunts using techniques that differ from one population to another, from beaching itself briefly to grab a seal to working with the rest of the group to herd fish into a tight ball, and none of this is instinctive; it is learned by watching and imitating. A calf stays at its mother's side for years to absorb this knowledge firsthand, following her on hunts long before it is skilled enough to catch anything on its own. What keeps the bond going so long is not the body's development but the sheer amount there is to learn.
